## What doing it consciously looks like

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.

Before making love, I want to know enough about the hard stuff that I’m not finding it all out after I’m bonded. Jealousy, attraction to other people, what happens under stress, old patterns, how recent the healing is, what each of us wants when things go bad, money. But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation.

That doesn’t mean I want ten profound talks in one weekend. At some point I’m mostly learning what she says about herself. Then I need ordinary time. And if I keep getting a little “wait” feeling, that doesn’t prove anything either. But if I’m about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that’s enough reason for me to ask it.

Sex can also start answering questions it has no business answering. We sleep together, moving in starts feeling obvious, and then living together starts feeling like we already decided on the long term. I still wouldn’t move in too fast if I can avoid it, and I’d pick a date to check in before a crisis. Wanting somebody doesn’t tell me whether I should have children with her or build a life with her. One of the stupid things my brain can do is turn “I’m taking a chance on her” into “she’s the right person” after we’ve been together for a while. Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something. Sometimes nothing changed except that now I’m attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.

I’d also try to make some real friends together. My friends are going to hear me first and hers are going to hear her first. That’s normal; they’re our friends. The problem is when every person around the relationship only knows one of us well. Then the first serious conflict turns into two teams arguing about two different relationships.

And don’t stop your own practices just because you’re in love. If I stop reparenting and meditating because my partner makes me feel okay, then she’s doing part of that job for me whether we say so or not.

## What doing it consciously looks like

Most of this I learned by getting it wrong. A few parts I’m still not sure about.

The first problem is that once I’m bonded, I hear things differently. So before making love I want some idea what I’m actually getting into: jealousy, attraction to other people, stress, old patterns, recent healing, money, what each of us wants from the other when things go bad. I don’t get much from asking for the correct philosophy. Put a real situation around it and ask what you think you’d actually do.

Then quit asking questions for a while. Ten profound conversations in one weekend can make me feel like I know somebody when mostly I know what she says about herself. I need boring time too. If I have a little “wait” feeling, it may be nothing. I still want to know what I was about to ignore before I keep going.

The next problem is one decision dragging the next one with it. Sex happens, so moving in feels natural. Once we live together, staying has practical momentum of its own. I’d rather not move in too fast if I have a choice, and I’d pick a date to check in before we need a crisis to force the conversation. Wanting her romantically also doesn’t answer whether I should have children with her or build my life with her. My brain can turn “I’m taking a chance on her” into “she’s the right person” without much new evidence. Sometimes all that changed is that I got more attached.

Meanwhile I want people around who know us together. My friends hear me first; hers hear her first. Fine. They’re our friends. But if nobody knows both of us, the first serious conflict becomes two teams arguing about two different relationships.

And I keep reparenting and meditating when I’m in love. If I stop because my partner makes me feel okay, then she’s doing part of that job for me whether we say so or not.

## What doing it consciously looks like

I learned most of this by screwing it up, so this is less a system than stuff I wish I had remembered.

Before making love, I want to know enough about the hard things that I’m not hearing all of them for the first time after I’m bonded. Jealousy. Other attractions. What she does under stress. Old patterns and how recent the healing really is. Money. What she wants from me when she’s having a terrible day. Asking somebody what they believe about those things is only partly useful; I’d rather put an actual situation around the question.

Then I need to stop interviewing her and actually live some life together. Ten profound conversations can tell me we’re good at profound conversations. A boring Tuesday tells me something else. So does the little “wait” feeling I’m tempted to ignore because I want the relationship to work. It might be wrong. I still want to ask what it’s about.

I also don’t want sex to quietly decide that we should live together, or living together to quietly decide that she’s my life partner. If I can avoid moving in early, I will. If we do live together, I want a check-in date before a crisis. And wanting somebody doesn’t tell me whether I should have children with her or build a life with her. “I’m taking a chance on her” can turn into “she’s the right person” just because now I’m attached.

I’d make friends together too. My old friends will be partial to me and hers to her. That’s normal. But I’ve already seen what happens when the relationship has two separate teams and nobody who knows us both.

And I keep my own practices. Being loved is exactly when it becomes easy to forget that I still have to reparent and regulate myself.
